utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Please have the accused brought in, Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Does everybody hear? Does the Prosecution hear? Does the Defence hear? Mr. Nobilo? Mr. Hayman? Mr. Blaskic, do you hear me? GENERAL BLASKIC: Good morning, your Honours. I hear you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, do you hear? MR.. CAYLEY: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning. Before I give you the floor, Mr. Cayley, I would like to make a comment about a point which is of great concern to this Trial Chamber, more specifically to the presiding judge speaking to you. I am referring to the translation problem. I understand the difficulties experienced by the translation service and can share their concerns as well. Nonetheless the French language is one of the working languages of this Tribunal. I do know that it would be an absolutely Utopian situation if they only had English, but unfortunately French is one of the working languages at this Tribunal, and I am doing a lot of work in English and making progress thanks to you. Still, to speak more seriously about this issue, I think that we must try to solve this problem. I know for you this is a very difficult issue. For instance I can point out to you that I have still not received a translation into French. I still do not have a French translation of one of the protective measures for the witnesses that one of the parties suggested last week. It is not a very long document, perhaps a page and a half. I was able to read it thanks to the help from my colleagues. I believe beyond the point of understanding it myself I think it would be proper for all documents to be translated into French. That is the first point. The second has to do with all of the documents. I think that there is a significant amount of work, and I'm convinced that we have to find an agreement. I believe that thanks to the help of my colleagues I can say to you there is a way of reaching an agreement. Nonetheless this cannot be done without extra people working in the French section in the translation service at this Tribunal. I do not want to say anything else about it, because we do have a trial here, but it is part of the trial that the documents are communicated properly. Perhaps we do not have to translate everything, but once again I have to tell you we have to come to an agreement. I want to find one. I ask you to speak with the translation service and its chiefs so next week we can have a small meeting in order to find out a way to solve this problem and find out what can be done, both in principle. There are certain things which must be done as regards the principle beyond the understanding of this judge, because the trials we are conducting here are for history. In 20, 30 or 40 years people have to be able to go back to the traces of the Tadic, Blaskic or Celebici trial in both of the official languages of this Tribunal. This has to do with moving legal knowledge forward. Also what is involved are the facts within this trial that come out and the three judges must be able to operate normally and starting with the very person speaking to you, who is handicapped by being French but can do nothing about it, and therefore must work in his own language. Therefore, after having made this little joke, I would like to take up things more seriously once again. I can give you back the floor, Mr. Cayley, so I think you can have once again Professor Pajic brought in. Thank you. MR.. CAYLEY: Mr. President, your Honours, learned counsel, good morning. The Office of the Prosecutor, Mr. President, fully appreciates your wishes in respect of translations and indeed, as you say, they do have historic and important consequences. Specifically in request of the five items yesterday that were not fully translated into the French language, I spoke with Monsieur Gilbert of the translation unit. He is working on those at the moment and hopefully you will have them within a short period of time. I will, as you have requested, make arrangements for a meeting so that these problems can be solved. Lastly, I would like to publicly say thank you to the translation unit for all of the work they have done on these particular documents. It has been a very difficult task, as the language is highly technical. They have done an extraordinarily good job. I would just like to take this opportunity to thank him for that work. The second matter, Mr. President, is another matter of procedure, and that concerns exhibits. I would like to now formally request before the witness is brought in that certain items be admitted into evidence that the Prosecutor did not request during the proceedings. If there are no objections from the Defence, I can number those items off, and I think the Registrar's officer is aware of the documents I'm speaking of. I would like admitted into evidence documents 36 A, B, C and D. Those are the original versions of the Narodni lists. Item 38, A, B and C, which are respectively the Serbo-Croat, the Croatian extract of the documents selected by Dr. Pajic; the French extract and the English extract.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Does the Defence agree? MR.. HAYMAN: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Therefore, we ask the Registrar to have these documents numbered as requested by Mr. Cayley. I give you have the floor again, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. One last matter. The witness, Dr. Pajic, is expecting to leave this evening. Now, the Office of the Prosecutor fully respects my learned friend's right to cross-examine the witness, as indeed is General Blaskic's right under the Statute, but in that sense he wished me personally to communicate that to you, that he would be expecting to leave the Tribunal this evening for business in London. With that, your Honour, and with your permission, could I call the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: As regards the last point, I believe that the Tribunal cannot make any commitments, because the cross-examination will take place under whatever conditions that the Defence wants. You were able to ask as many questions as you like, and the Defence must be able to do the same. We all hope that this will allow Professor Pajic to leave this evening, but if he cannot, I do not think we will do what we did for another witness, who didn't begin, but this time I think we have to conclude. That's the only thing I can say as things stand now. Please have the Professor brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor. Do you hear me? Have you rested up a bit and everything all right? Fine. Then this morning you have a few more comments to which you are being asked to respond, comments from the Prosecution, and then the Defence will ask you some questions. Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Dr. Pajic, we left off yesterday at the end of yesterday's session with you discussing the final documents in the extract which concern the decision of the Constitutional Court in Sarajevo, and I stated yesterday that you wished to make some concluding remarks as a finish to your examination-in-chief. If you could now go ahead and make your concluding remarks, viewing all of the documents as a whole and employing your expertise to explain to the judges as fully as you can your overall view of these documents. Thank you, Dr. Pajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (In interpretation): since my analysis covered a large number of documents published in the Official Gazette and a few documents that were not in that publication, perhaps it might be useful for me to summarise my expert opinion. Regarding the methodology of this summary, let me say that I shall try to be brief, and, secondly, I have divided my conclusions into two parts. I will first make four individual conclusions and end up with the general conclusion regarding the normative activities of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which later became the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. My first conclusion of an individual nature is as follows. A community of municipalities was formed known as the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and gradually by its normative activities it acquired the attributes of statehood. From the very beginning all the documents of the HZ H-B insist on territorial integrity and the Defence of territorial integrity as one of the main attributes of statehood. All the municipalities of HZ H-B are municipalities within the territory of the sovereign Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the course of the emergence of the Croatian Community is systematically ignored as a State. Its competencies are marginalised. Its constitutional system is ignored, and the legislation of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina violated. In fact, autonomous bodies of authority are established and an independent legal order is built up of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. What is more, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna took over part of the frontier of Bosnia-Herzegovina and regulated independently the frontier regime which in formal and legal terms belongs to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. My second conclusion is as follows. Through all the documents that I have analysed, like a thread one notices the omnipresent role of the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, in all state affairs. May I recall that the HVO was set up as the supreme body of defence of the Croatian Community, but already in the first document it acquired a decisive role in the Presidency of the Croatian Community, which was defined as the legislative body of the Croatian Community. In this connection one immediately notices the unity of functions held by one individual, that is the President of the Croatian Community, who is at the same time the President of the Croatian Defence Council. The Croatian Defence Council is constituted as a supreme executive and administrative authority, with the characteristics of a government. The HVO covers the departments of Defence, the Interior, the Economy, Finance, Social Affairs, Justice an Administration through appropriate departments headed by appointed chiefs. Gradually the Croatian Defence Council encompasses control over the functioning of the system of the judiciary, primarily the Prosecutor's Offices and the courts, the regular courts. It appoints and relieves judges within that judicial system. In brief, the Croatian Defence Council is concentrating within its control the legislative, administrative and executive powers. At the same time the Croatian Defence Council preserves all the prerogatives of a supreme defence body, and it is based on a principle of subordination at the national level, without any right of the municipalities to set up their own bodies at municipal level. My third conclusion is that the Defence of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna from the beginning was entrusted to the Croatian Defence Council. The Defence of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was organised on the basis of the principle of the participation of all citizens in defence. In the decision that is I described over the past few days, a system was elaborated whereby each citizen of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna knows or can know what his obligations are with respect to defence either as a conscript, or if he comes under the obligation to work, or if he has to contribute in financial or material resources to the activities of defence. The HVO is the absolute supervisor and holder and proprietor of all the acquired material goods. In this connection the entire production for the needs of the military comes under the control of the HVO, which also supervises the work of public enterprises. The armed forces of the Croatian Community are gradually set up through the documents I have referred to as a legally founded structure, with emphasis on the unity of command and subordination and disciplinary responsibility, which is accompanied by a system of military courts. My fourth conclusion of this nature is that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was established as a national entity aspiring to round off a certain territory, whether legitimately or not -- which I'm not entering into because that is not my field of expertise -- a territory that would correspond to the interests of the Croatian people in this area. In addition to all the institutions of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which later became the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, the attribute of "Croatian" is emphasised. Though at the moment it was formed the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in all the 30 municipalities enumerated in the first decision on its establishment, there are members of other ethnic groups, with the exception of four municipalities: Posusje, Siroki Brijeg, Grude and Citluk, where representatives of other ethnic groups are very few, in all the other, that is in the 26 out of the 30 municipalities, there are inhabitants belonging to other ethnic groups, Muslims and Serbs, or Muslims or Serbs, and their share in the population varies. According to the 1991 census, it varies from 72-82 per cent depending on the municipalities. However, in spite of this, all the regulations in their wording, as well as in the rhetoric used, implicitly exclude the non-Croat population from the political life of the Croatian Community. The institutions of the system of authority are constituted in such a way that only representatives of the Croatian people are represented. I must say in addition to all this that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and later the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna did not pass a single legal regulation that would guarantee the rights of minorities in accordance with international standards, and especially not of national religious and ethnic and linguistic minorities. This is no coincidence, because in some documents a general readiness is expressed to accept and observe the Geneva conventions and General international law. Finally allow me to make a very general conclusion in a few words. I have read and analysed a large number of documents. I think that I had in total either at home and in my offices both ten and 12 kilograms of documents to study. I must say that, as a lawyer, I immediately noticed one characteristic. These documents, with very few exceptions, are the product of highly skilled legal qualities. One immediately notices a number of principles. First, the gradual character of the normative activities; secondly, the continuity in that normative activity; then also the systematic nature of the regulations and decisions, their consistency. I have indicated on several occasions a few minor points where one notices any contradictions. In brief, one clearly notices the tendency to expand state prerogatives during 1992 and 1993, and something that impresses me in particular in view of the fact that I know the conditions under which the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna emerged, that is conditions of more or less wartime environment, depending on the time, is the comprehensiveness of these normative activities. I was frequently surprised to come across documents of the following contents. Let me cite a few as an illustration. For example, the adoption of the decree on founding a Motoring Club of the Croatian Community; a decree confirming the Statute of the Motoring Club and on the appointment of the secretary-general of the Motoring Club. These were all published in the Official Gazette number 5 of 1992 signed by the President of the HVO. Then the decree on the establishment and work of the University in Mostar, which was also published in the Official Gazette number 6 of 1992, with a provision saying that the Chancellor is responsible to the HVO. Then in Official Gazette number 7 of 1992 a decision on the appointment of the Deans of various departments of the Mostar University. Then in the Official Gazette number 8 of 1992 a decree on games, on lotteries. Then on the foundation of the fire brigades, again in the Official Gazette of 1993. Then a decree on the foundation of the Geophysical Institute in the Official Gazette Number 6 of 1993. I could list many more examples, which are all illustrative of the comprehensiveness of those normative activities and the intention of the legislator to cover also social affairs by specific legal regulations of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Thank you, Mr. President, for your attention. With that I complete my analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, have you any other questions before we give the floor to Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour. We can offer the witness for cross-examination continuity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: May I inform the court how we intend to proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo will commence the cross-examination. I will also have a smaller number of questions. I wanted to assure the Tribunal in advance we will exercise the greatest care not to duplicate questions, but for reasons of both linguistics and subject matter, we feel it is important that we both have the opportunity to ask questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hayman. The Tribunal has no problem with that. Both of you represent the Defence and you organise General Blaskic's defence as you intend to do, as you like,, but of course, respecting the conditions set by the Tribunal. Mr. Nobilo, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, your Honours, learned counsel. Dr. Pajic, my name is Anto Nobilo, defence counsel of General Blaskic, and I would like to ask you a few questions. Let us go back to the beginning of your statement. We won't take so long, of course, but your first assertion which I noticed was that for the states of the European tradition and the former Yugoslavia, it was characteristic to issue official gazettes in which laws and other regulations are published, and that that is one of the indications of the statehood of Herceg-Bosna. Have I remembered well your submission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Basically yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I should like to remind you, do you not recall that even today and in the former Yugoslavia cities and municipalities also had their official gazettes, where city councils published their decisions and regulations governing life in the towns; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Therefore in view of this one could not claim that only states had official gazettes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true, but I was actually concentrating on the contents of the legal regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, but you spoke of the form, the existence of an Official Gazette as a publication for official documents, and I am now referring to this form, the method of publication of regulations, and saying that cities also have some forms, that is such official gazettes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us go on. Then you said that the first decision on the establishment of Herceg-Bosna was passed on 18th December 1991, but that the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina had still not started at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I should like to remind you that between 18th and 20th September 1992, 10,000 reservists from Serbia and Montenegro came to Bosnia-Herzegovina in the area of Stoliz, Heliodom. They didn't enter the barracks, but immediately took up positions in the field in the direction of Neum and western Herzegovina, and those were the first foreign troops in the beginning of the invasion. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as my memory serves me, because we are now talking about facts --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, but it was important to know what was the environment within which certain documents were passed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, let me say the following. First of all, I do not deny that even in that period there was a certain pre-war psychosis in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I myself was a witness of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And in Croatia it was already war.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. President, could I make an objection please? The witness must be given time to actually answer the question, and at the moment Dr. Pajic is trying to answer and as soon as he is, Mr. Nobilo is actually talking over him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I find this objection is well founded. Ask your questions, take as long as you like to ask the question, but then allow the witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a war psychosis in Bosnia-Herzegovina even in this period we are referring to now. On the other hand, I'm not quite sure that I could agree with your description of foreign troops, because at that time the Yugoslav People's Army still existed in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and as far as I remember there was a regional command in Sarajevo of the JNA at the time. I'm not going to enter into discussions as to what they were preparing, but they were co-operating with the legal authorities of the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But do you agree that it was visible that the war was in the offing in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would agree with that. I myself made a public statement somewhere in January 1992, saying that I feared there would be war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but for various reasons and looking to the international community too, we had hoped that the war would be prevented.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember that on 20th September 1991 the village of Ravna was razed to the ground? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was linked to the operations near Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the territory of Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I should like to ask is it for you normal somebody should prepare for defence before war breaks out, or is it better and more normal for them to prepare for defence when the war actually begins?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only say if only we had prepared in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So can we view this document as one of the ways -- I'm not saying the only one -- to prepare for defence against the aggressor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I would not agree with you, because the decision to establish the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna only partially speaks of the need for defending the Croatian Community. It doesn't explicitly say that an aggression is being prepared or a war against The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That is my problem. May I then draw your attention to point two of the Prosecutor's file? Perhaps you could look up those documents. It will be easier. Exhibit 38. I point to page 2. It is the decision establishing the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are talking about the revised text?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second one then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Perhaps if we follow the same numbers, it will be easier. So when you were talking about this decision, I think that you did not exactly indicate the reasons for the establishment. Here they are explicitly stated. I should like to read them to you and to hear your comments. The reasons for the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and it says: "Faced with the ruthless aggression of the Yugoslav Army and Chetniks against The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and The Republic of Croatia, with a tremendous number of lives lost, with the suffering and pain, with the fact that age-old Croatian territories and goods are being coveted, with the destruction of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its legally elected bodies, the Croatian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina in these difficult moments of their history, etc., are establishing the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna". Can you comment on this? Do you accept that these were the main reasons that are put here as the reasons for the establishment of the Croatian Community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, you have read to me the preamble of a decision that was passed on 3rd July 1992, when the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina was well underway, but the decision on the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is stated 18th November 1991, and to it is attached a short preamble, too, which differs in many respects from the preamble that you will find in the revised text. Maybe we can read it and we can again see the reasons for the establishment of the community, if you agree. I'm talking about this sentence that you emphasised. If we read this decision, noting the date, 3rd July 1992, then I quite agree with you that this preamble is acceptable, that is faced with the ruthless aggression of the Yugoslav army and Chetniks against The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and The Republic of Croatia. However, the preamble corresponding to the text of 18th, there is no reference to the ruthless aggression to the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: As I was saying the, Yugoslav army in Bosnia-Herzegovina still existed, but if you look at the preamble of the first document, you will see in the first sentence: "At moments when the last Communist army in Europe together with the Chetniks is threatening the survival of the Croatian State and Croatian people", which implies also the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Communist army is the JNA and the Chetniks are the Chetniks. Does this also not indicate the reason, only later on it is much clearer, of course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a matter of interpretation. I think your interpretation is rather extensive, rather broad, because if we are talking about threats to the survival of the Croatian state and the Croatian people, Bosnia-Herzegovina is not mentioned in that context. It is later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But it says: "We, the elected representatives of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina". Not to dwell on this matter, do you agree or disagree with me that the reason for the establishment of this entity or whatever you like to call it, that the main reason was the danger of war, the need to organise defence of the territory which the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina feel they are entitled to where they live. Do you agree that that was the main reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would agree, yes, to organise and prepare defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes. So we have come to an agreement. I should now like to ask you to recall what the Federal Government at the end of 1991 -- when I say the Federal Government, I am thinking of the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- what did it do to prepare for defence? Did the Federal Government protect its citizens, the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, against aggression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are asking me a question which I cannot answer on the basis of these documents, you see. We could engage in a discussion which would be reminiscent of memoirs. This is a period five years ago, and I could talk to you on the basis of my own memory. I was not a member of the government of the Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to object again, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: As you can see, Mr. Nobilo is covering wide-ranging areas well outside the essence of the testimony of the witness. Dr. Pajic came here to testify upon the basis of the documents that are before learned counsel for the Defence, that are before yourselves. He was not brought here to testify on these huge political events that were going on Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, and I would request that Mr. Nobilo's cross-examination is limited to the documents and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, do you want to add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the direct examination at various times went outside the documents and the context for these events, to the extent this witness has personal knowledge, and please recall this witness left Sarajevo in 1992. He has some personal knowledge. I do not believe there is going to be extensive questioning here but some questioning, I submit, should be allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to consult with my colleagues for a moment. (Pause) We are overruling the objection, but we request that the Defence remain concise and to focus more on the documents themselves. Thank you. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You do not have to repeat the question. I can answer. On the reservation that I'm speaking truly only on the basis of personal impressions, that I do not have in my possession any documents from this domain of my statement, I can say that the Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time when the war fully broke out was highly impeded. The State territory was fragmentised to a large extent. The communications were broken off all over throughout The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then to the best of my knowledge then in Sarajevo people started being involved in self-organisations. Some areas were defended better and some worse. I can only speak from my personal experience in Sarajevo, which defended itself from invasion. Whether this was done by the well-organised, prepared-in-advance army of Bosnia-Herzegovina I do not know, but it is for sure had there not been an organised defence, Sarajevo would have fallen into the hands of the Yugoslav People's Army or later the units that took over the JNA armaments and equipment and held Sarajevo to siege. One should not forget before the war broke out -- whenever I speak of the beginning of the war, please understand me; I mean April 1992 -- one should not forget that considerably before that date in Bosnia-Herzegovina the units of the United Nations armed forces were deployed, UNPROFOR, and rightfully so or less rightfully so a lot of people were hoping that UNPROFOR would stop war breaking out in Bosnia-Herzegovina and contribute to the preservation of peace. Unfortunately all our hopes were in vain and all circumstances point to the fact that it's difficult to speak of a comprehensive defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was fragmentised. In some places it was more successful, like in Tuzla, and in some places less successful like in Western Herzegovina, etc.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Mr. Nobilo's microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I agree with you, but we should highlight one thing. If it was necessary to have self-organisation, is it not that a negation of a system of organisation of the Federal Government or shortcomings in the Federal Government itself. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, if we are going to talk about the necessity of defence only, we could agree on that, but I remind you of Article 1 of the decision on establishing the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. No reference is made to defence. It said that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna shall be established as a political, cultural, economic and territorial integrity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But in the reasons for establishing it defence is truly referred to, and you said later that the military acts drawn up were very good from the legal point of view, but let us go back to the fate of the man in the street in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the defence claims that they were not protected by the authorities and they should have been protected by the authorities, your fate. According to our information you have left Sarajevo some time in mid-1992. Was that for reasons of security or rather insecurity in terms of your life in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I shared the fate of all the people of Sarajevo, so yes, that is one of the reasons. Another reason is that my activity by its very nature is that of a public figure, an independent intellectual, and in Sarajevo I felt rather isolated from the rest of the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Exactly. So can we conclude on that basis that your government did not give you enough security for your work and communications?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you know in conditions of war an individual should not expect too much from his or her government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Everyone is the master of his fate. I agree with you the Croatian people didn't expect that much and they also took their destiny in their own hands. So let us proceed. The next assertion which I would like to dispute a bit, that is that this organisation was not in keeping with the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I would agree with you on that, but could you explain at the point in time when the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was established in November 1991 what the constitution was still in force in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a good question, because nearing the end of the last regime in Bosnia-Herzegovina there was a confusion in terms of the legal and constitutional situation. So when it was certain that the former regime which was headed by the former League of Communists of Yugoslavia was losing the ground under its feet certain changes were made, first of all in the constitutions of the republics, and, of course, the constitution that was valid then was the first constitution from 1974, both the federal constitution and the republican constitution. However, it was amended considerably in 1988 and 1989. I am speaking of the constitution of The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Immediately upon the establishment of the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina after the first multi-party elections, work was done on elaborating a new constitution. This took quite a bit of time but at the beginning of 1991 numerous amendments were adopted, and they legally sanctioned the existing situation, namely a multi-party system, the composition of the Parliament, the composition of the government and also the composition of the Presidency as the collective head of state. So in response to your question I can say that the old constitution from 1974 was in force with the amendments from 1988, 1989, and 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I have understood that these amendments changed in a sense -- touched upon the question of the multi-party quality of the country, but in terms of Yugoslavia in November 1991 Bosnia was still part of Yugoslavia a federal unit of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have a text of the constitution here but I am almost certain that that was so for the simple reason that The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina had not yet become independent in an international legal sense of the word. As you know, after the conclusions passed by the Badinter Commission on behalf of the European Community, then it was envisaged that the republics that wished to attain independence on the territory of the former Yugoslavia were supposed to carry out a referendum on that. It is only after that referendum in March 1992 that the first international recognitions of Bosnia-Herzegovina started coming in as an independent state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So we can conclude in terms of the first decision on establishment in November 1991 and the second one in July 1992 Bosnia was still within the framework of Yugoslavia at least from the point of view of law and constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But in April? You said that Bosnia was internationally recognised in the summer; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. In the first week of April 1992 it was recognised and it was -- it became a member of the United Nations the same day as Croatia, on 22nd May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What is the army according to this valid constitution -- was the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and all other republics of Yugoslavia legally, formally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Legally, formally, the functioning army, so to speak, was the Yugoslav people's army, with highlighted elements of territorial defence because this was important in the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who was in charge of the territorial defence in the case of immediate threat of war or war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In such cases JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do we not have a constitutional paradox that the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was in the state of attacking Bosnia-Herzegovina as a State?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This question can only be understood in the context of national divisions that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We are talking constitutionally and legally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That came into being in Bosnia-Herzegovina, because constitutionally and legally that was the status of the JNA, as you have said. However, in fact, in the units of the JNA a lot of the military started leaving the units, those belonging to the Muslim and Croat ethnic groups, as you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, that is true, but formally, legally, when the fighting broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the JNA was the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you not think that in such a constitutional paradox, when an army attacks its own state, formally, legally constitutionally -- we know what it was like in real life -- one group of people or a group of municipalities, whatever you wish, do you not think that people or municipalities has the right on the basis of self-defence to violate certain constitutional provisions when we have such an anti-constitutional situation. What is more important there, formal violation of the constitution or the right to self-defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, ask your question and then allow the witness to answer, because you keep adding one question to the next before the witness can answer. Is your question different from mine, Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No, from President. I would simply echo what you are saying. Mr. Nobilo must have respect for the witness and allow him to answer the questions, otherwise the process becomes ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There is a technical complication here. You are speaking very quickly. Interpreters are going as best they can, but at some point while you are concluding your question, the witness is answering, and it is not really very convenient. I think it would be simpler in order to help the work of the judges and the work of the interpreters to ask your question, allow the witness to answer, and then continue asking further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, and I accept the objections that were made. However, one thing I cannot accept, that I do not show due respect to the expert witness. I think that we're having a fine conversation. You were in the process of replying, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before I give a resolute answer to your question what is the priority, I have to remind you of the context in which all of this was happening. It is quite clear that the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina are seeking ways of defending themselves from aggression. However, I wish to remind you that at the same time when we are talking about this decision, one version and the other, accelerated work is being done in the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo on negotiations for the JNA to leave Bosnia-Herzegovina. Active participation is taken in these negotiations by Mr. Jerko Dojko, Minister of Defence, who was nominated to this post as the candidate of the political party of the Croatian Democratic Union. I know him personally, and that is why I have such detailed information. So preparations are underway for the evacuation of the JNA, that is the terminology that was used then, from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is the delicate point in time when at the same time the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was in the process of being established, and if you remember then, General Sebir -- I can't remember his first name -- was appointed commander of the General staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, but you didn't answer whether the violation of the constitution or the right to self-defence are more important. What is the basic right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is an academic question. I agree with you that the right to self-defence is a basic right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I also wish to draw your attention to another thing. You have spoken in detail about the decision on establishing the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. That is page 2, point two, but perhaps you did not emphasise Article 5 fully. I wish to draw your attention to that and read it out to you: "The community shall respect the democratically elected bodies of authorities of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina so long as the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina remains independent from the former or any future Yugoslavia"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you for having reminded me of this provision. I think it is important for interpreting the overall aspirations of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. This provision truly says that the community shall respect the democratically elected Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina as long as the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina remains independent from the former or any future Yugoslavia. This is a provision of a conditional nature, I would say, conditional nature, but a condition which was counted upon, but it was never truly met, because you would agree with me that in the dramatic events that followed, Bosnia and Herzegovina got out of Yugoslavia and so far it has not entered a future Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Exactly, and this territory is still in Bosnia-Herzegovina until the present day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Okay. So I go on. Also you asserted that the decision on page 2, the definite text on the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in relation to the first decision on establishing the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna goes a step further in terms of emphasising elements of statehood. So I ask you what was the situation like in the military sense in September 1992 or July 1992? Although you already replied to that in comparison to 1992, I am not asking you for details. Worse or better?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now I wish to draw your attention to page 4 of point two, evidence 38. We have a decision of the Croatian Defence Council, an important decision I would agree with you. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: For the Tribunal, specifically point out which document you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This is document number 2 of the Prosecutor's evidence, page 4. Perhaps in the French translation it is different, but in English and in Croatian it is page 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When speaking of that decision, I think that you omitted the preamble, so I ask you for your comment after I read it: "Pursuant to Article 7 of the decision establishing Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna" -- now this is what I wish to highlight -- "faced with aggression in the territories of the Croatian communities of Herceg-Bosna and the fact that the Croatian people have been left unprotected, aware of the impotence of the legal authorities of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in particular the disintegration of its defence system, at its emergency session of 8th April 1992 issues the following ...", etc., etc. Could you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What is missing, lacking here in this preamble, if you are asking me for my opinion, is the following. I would expect from the point of view of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna to express the assessment that this is aggression on the territory of all of Bosnia-Herzegovina. As you know very well from the census in 1991, the members of the Croatian people live throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not only the 30-odd municipalities included in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. That is why I believe that there is this shortcoming here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: All right, but do you accept the rest, that these were the main reasons why the HVO was established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the point of view of defence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now we are reaching a key point in your expert opinion, and I think that we have to pay attention to that and spend some more time on that. This Croatian defence council which is established as the supreme defence body of the Croatian people, is it of civilian or military nature? Is it an army or is it a civilian organisation? Can you define that according to this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that it is still premature to establish such a definition on the basis of this document only and one or two or three Articles. However, it is important to recall something that I've said probably over these last few days, that in Article 2 it is not only said that the Croatian people will be defended, but also the sovereign space of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. In my opinion, the sovereign space or territorial integrity is a far more concrete notion as far as statehood is concerned than the interests of a particular national or ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I agree with you, but I also wish to draw your attention to the fact that in Article 2 reference is not only made to the protection of the Croatian people, but also other peoples in the community who live on the territory of the community. So it's not only protection of the Croat people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This definition is clear. This is the protection of the sovereignty of the space of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I can agree to that but let us leave that aside. Can you tell me whether this document is sufficient for you or not to say whether this is an army, a military or a civilian organ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to this decision, it is a civilian authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go on. Our next page, page 5. We come to the statutory decision on the temporary organisation of executive authority and administration in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. You have said generally that the HVO as a military structure comes to head the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and in a way this military structure governs the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Croatian Defence Council as a defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: There is a difference involved. It is a defence structure. Is it a military structure or can it be a civilian defence structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It can be a civilian defence structure in view of the fact how the units were established and the municipal HVOs, how they were established. This was a military organisation after all. You know that very well, because this was the organisation of the defence of the Croatian people on the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you believe that the establishment of the HVO in the municipalities was basically a military structure and on that basis you draw the conclusion that the HVO was a military structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see on the basis of these documents at the very outset the HVO is clearly defined as a defence structure, and it is said invariably that it is the supreme body of the Defence of the Croat people of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I'm speaking about the first document, the supreme defence body. However, you said according to that document it was a civilian structure after all. Then you said that the HVO in the municipalities was basically a military structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I can tell you from my personal experience that in certain municipalities in Sarajevo HVO units were established where people in uniform appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Dr. Pajic, we who lived there are all aware of it, and we know it, and even people on the outside have been informed. Military units and the executive and administrative authority of Herceg-Bosna used the same name, but it is not the same thing, and you have asserted a different thing here. I draw your attention to the statutory decision of the municipal authorities. You did not choose that document in your compilation. I can have it translated later and submitted as evidence. I can quote it to you now. In your translations it is also there. With your permission, you could have a look at it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Has this already been submitted as evidence? It is already part of the trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, it was submitted but it was not translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, all right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is 36 A, page 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Professor would like to make a comment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I referred to this statutory decision that Mr. Nobilo is referring to on municipal authorities. I have it here in my volume, statutory decision on municipal executive authorities and administrative bodies. May 15th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. So it's page 9. Article 1. Article 1 defines that executive authority, I repeat executive authority, that falls within the rights and obligations of the municipalities, and we know what the municipalities and cities did, shall be exercised by the municipal Croatian Defence Council. Therefore, isn't the municipal Croatian Defence Council a civilian structure, after all, because if you go on further you can read the entire statutory decision on page 9. It is obvious that this is a municipal executive body, which simply has a different name. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So it is a civilian structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is a civilian structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So from in point of view the HVO is a civilian structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in a sense it is of a civilian structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, I think this is the time you take a break. For the sake of understanding, I insist we must take into account the work of the interpreters. You both speak the same language but I think for all of us using the interpretation it is very complicated. You have to make it clear what is the question and what is the answer. I believe that we can now take a break and we will resume in fifteen minutes at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing can now resume. Have the accused brought in and have the witness brought in as well, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is a simple point and a matter that has been raised by the translation unit. Because Mr. Nobilo, and I'm sure it is not deliberate, is not allowing the witness to always answer the question before he begins with another question, the translation is just running into itself and the transcript is not very well. So they have asked if he could pause between actually the witness answering the question and him asking another question, because otherwise the whole thing becomes uncontrollable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Riad, would like to make a commentary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I follow the translation and it is difficult to know, because it is the same voice, so sometimes we think it is the continuation. So perhaps the interpreter can say "question", "answer", so we know it is the answer. It is the same voice and the same tone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I will allow myself to intervene for a second. In the French transcript frequently one says "question", "answer". The difficulty that the Prosecutor is pointing out and I did as well stems from two facts. Mr. Nobilo or Mr. Hayman or Mr. Cayley himself here talking about Serbo-Croat, there has to be a little bit of time because theoretically even if we can congratulate the great skill of our interpreters, there is some time lag. Therefore, the distinction has to be made between question and answer. They have tried very hard this morning. The interpreters have put in question and answer. Mr. Nobilo, please be careful to be more disciplined. I know you are very much taken by your subject. You have to show some discipline. The question raised by the Prosecutor is a good one. The transcript has to reflect the difference between the questions and the answers. Based on that and the indications given by Judge Riad, we can now go on. Mr. Nobilo, I give you the floor once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Of course, it takes a little time to adjust to this multi-lingual environment, but I'll do my best. Dr. Pajic, I think we ended with the conclusion -- please correct me if I'm wrong -- that the municipal HVOs were actually civilian organs of authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In formal and legal terms yes, but in the context of the overall defence preparations certainly the HVO later on assumes certain functions. As we can see from the documents, certain decisions at the national level are signed by the President of the HVO relative to military matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That is correct, but you probably remember that in the former Yugoslavia in the municipalities there were defence secretariats. There was a Secretariat of the Interior. Were these civilian or military or police structures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were organs of the administration, therefore civilian. Let me try and make a pause before providing the answer. That division was not reflected in the legal documents. We used the following terminology: administrative organs of authority, military organs, legislative organs. We did not have that kind of a division in the legal documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But when you say administrative bodies of authority, that is not a military body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, but in the context of the overall organisation of the HVO I insist that the HVO did have definite military competencies. I repeat, and I have indicated repeatedly, that all decisions relative to the defence of the country were signed by the President of the HVO and later on the head of the Defence Department of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I agree with you, but the question is: is he a civilian or a military man, because, of course, the civilian structure also has certain competencies with respect to defence. We will come to that, but what is essential is that a civilian structure or a military.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The persons I have mentioned, as far as I know, were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Dr. Pajic, let me try once again to take you back to page 5 of document number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It is true that in the French interpretation people -- the interpreter is saying "question", "answer", but in the English interpretation we do not hear the words "question", "answer". If the English booth could make that extra effort, it would be very much appreciated. Mr. Nobilo, take up again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I should like to take you back to exhibit 38, item 3, page 5, the statutory decision on the temporary organisation of executive authority. Article 1, is it according to you a definition of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Article 1 in my opinion defines the competencies of the HVO in the area of the executive and administrative competencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is that at the same time a definition of the HVO as a body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would agree, yes, it is to a considerable extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What does "to a considerable extent" mean? Is the HVO something outside the executive and the administration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here is why I have some reservation. You will remember from my analysis that the HVO participates in the Presidency which is defined as a legislative body. Then also you will see in later documents all documents relative to the establishment of the armed forces, the structure of the armed forces, were signed by the President of the HVO and in that respect the authorities of the HVO, the definition of the HVO is far broader than simply to say that it is a body of executive authority and administration in the territory of the Croatian communities of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I agree with you that the HVO has certain legislative powers, but as far as military powers are concerned, they emanate from Article 20, where the Defence Department is established as a part of the executive authority. Article 20 speaks about several departments and is the Defence Department in this article still a civilian or a military department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Defence Department is a civilian structure of the executive and administrative authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That is correct. Therefore, if we summarise all that you have said now regarding the nature of the HVO, can we conclude from that that the HVO, as well as the HVO members who were within the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, represent the civilian structure rather than the military, and that there was also the army, an armed force, bearing the same name, but which is not identical with the civilian HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I do not understand your question. I think it is of a rather speculative nature. We're trying to do guesswork regarding what is civilian and what is military.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Maybe you didn't understand me. Let me repeat myself. The HVO, as it is defined by the statutory decision on the temporary composition of executive authority, you agreed that it was a civilian body. You also agreed that the municipal HVO was a civilian body, and yesterday you asserted that the HVO was a military body, and that the army through HVO representatives was in the highest level leadership, that is in the Presidency, of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. These are two different conclusions on two different days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the interpretation of what I said is too broad. I did not say that the army was a component part of the Presidency, and if you claim that I did, then we'll have to look at the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt again. I have made this point to counsel, to Mr. Hayman. Mr. Nobilo is representing matters that the witness has said, and yet he doesn't refer to where in the transcript from yesterday these statements were made. It may be that there is a slight misrepresentation of what the witness actually stated yesterday, and I think now Dr. Pajic is actually indicating that. Mr. Nobilo must actually give some foundation to what he is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I agree. Mr. Nobilo, you are citing sources of the witness himself. Cite them properly, please. Yesterday, -- for example, you said that yesterday he said at this or this point this or that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I agree, but I have made a summary, something that emerges from his statement, so it is rather difficult, and I asked him whether that was correct, and only if he answers that it is, then I go on. If he says it is not correct, then I accept it. So I do not see any problem here. I'm not citing a particular statement, but what emerges from several pages of his statement. If he says that I misunderstood him, then I accept and we can go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I understand what you are saying, but in general terms you know you are particularly demanding, as is your colleague. When a source is cited by the Prosecutor, you always ask: "Where does the source come from? How does it come to be here?" I also have a comment to make. I do understand that in your manner of asking questions you refer to what the witness said and you expect the witness to say: "I did or didn't say something". The witness did answer if -- so the question has to do with interpretation. The Presiding Judge tends to think that yes, you should be more specific as to the place or places in yesterday's statement which appear subject to interpretation, which would be different to that from the witness. This is what I would like to say. Now go on but keep these observations in mind and be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I agree, but when we refer to sources that are not here, as opposed to sources that are here, who can confirm or reject what we are saying, and that is where the difference occurs, but I think as far as the nature of the HVO, we have sufficiently elucidated the question, and I'm satisfied. So I would now like you to look at page 12 of this same document and to look at the decree on the armed forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Within the framework of that decree please examine Article 61 on page 23. Page 23, Article 61, which says: "Members of the armed forces of the HZ H-B shall be held responsible for criminal, property and petty offences as stipulated by the regulations in force until the relevant bodies of the HZ H-B decide otherwise". On the basis of this Article I'm asking you the following question: General Blaskic, as the commander of the operative zone, on the basis of these regulations, what authority did he have in relation to his soldiers if that soldier commits a criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could you ask your question in more general terms, please? I am sorry to intervene, but not at one time yesterday was General Blaskic's responsibility invoked. If we understand correctly, you are speaking about the constitution, general, diplomatic, structural problems related to the HVO. Suddenly for purposes everybody understands you are bringing in the personal situation of General Blaskic. Personally I think that you must reformulate your question, ask it in more general terms. What is the criminal and material responsibility of those who are the leaders of the structure in question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I was doing this simply to make myself clear. I was thinking of a military commander in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. What authority did he have with respect to the criminal proceedings against his troops, because here it says that members of the armed forces shall be held responsible for criminal, property and other offences, as stipulated by regulations in force. Those regulations are the criminal code of the former SFRY and the criminal code of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, if you are familiar with these two codes, can you say what would be the responsibility of any military commander according to those regulations in force, if you can? This is in the area of criminal law. I realise that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The regulations you mention were not the subject of my analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. I should like to draw your attention to Article 23 of this same document. On page 17 of document 2 of Exhibit 38. This Article says: "Members of the armed forces shall observe in all circumstances when conducting covert operations the international laws of war on the humane treatment of the wounded or captured enemy, on the protection of the population and other provisions of these laws". Yesterday or the day before you alleged that this was typical of states. It seems to me that these are instructions addressed to the fighters of a particular military unit. Why would that have to be typical only of states? Any military unit or formation surely is obliged to respect international humanitarian law, and therefore the legislator is also duty bound to make such an obligation upon the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please formulate the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This obligation, is it the exclusive right of a state or can it be stipulated by any armed formation regarding its members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is one thing when an armed formation or the leadership of that armed formation reminds its troops of the general rules of international humanitarian law, and it is quite another matter when an entity in its legal documents provides a stipulation rather like a formal statement saying that members of the armed forces shall observe the international laws of war. This provision, in my view, is a highly generalised one, and it is customary, rather like a solemn declaration of a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can it not be interpreted as obliging the troops to behave accordingly? Can it not be interpreted in that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can interpret your question as implying that the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna which passed this decree is assuming, on the one hand, a commitment in relation to international law, and on the other hand, internally it commits itself to the observation of international humanitarian law by its armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Will you please now look at page 29, point two of Exhibit 38, which speaks about the enforcement of the law on misdemeanours? Actually you asserted that this was the beginning of the take-over of judicial powers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what I said, and that is what I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I should like to remind you that in the former Yugoslavia, as well as in Croatia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina, misdemeanour magistrates were part of the administrative authorities and not part of the judiciary in the organisational sense, the method of election and so on. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as far as the former Yugoslavia is concerned you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were there any new regulations passed in Bosnia regarding magistrates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Therefore, the magistrate judges were not part of the judiciary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only interpret your question as questioning my allegation that this was the first step towards the take-over of the judicial function. I was very precise in what I said. I did not claim that the system of magistrate courts was subordinated to the judiciary generally speaking but there is no doubt that this is an indication of the implementation for the responsibility of misdemeanours by the Croatian Community and the take-over of all the competence of the republican magistrate judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But you agree with me that the magistrate, including The Republic and magistrates for misdemeanours, were part not of the judiciary but of the administrative authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: A further point I should like to draw your attention to is the introduction of the Croatian Dinar in Herceg-Bosna. I should like to ask you: at the beginning of 1992 what currency was in use in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The currency in use at the time this decree was passed and that is July 1992 in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Dinar was the currency in use, which all of us called the Bosnian Dinar. True enough for your information no new bank notes were issued, but the old Yugoslav Dinar bank notes were used, which the authorities of the new Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina had restamped. Maybe it's not easy to translate this. Anyway, they placed on it a stamp, a seal of the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina for practical reasons, that it may be used in payments in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: From which month of 1992, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: If the Yugoslav bank notes were essentially in use, it was easy to carry out some sort of monetary blows because war was imminent, and wasn't there a real danger of that happening, and didn't that happen? Let us remember the monetary incursions made during the Government of Anto Markovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I am sorry to interrupt, but learned counsel is making a speech. He's not asking a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I didn't catch the interpretation here. Could we have the interpretation, please? Would you shorten your questions, please, make better summaries of what you have to say and then we'll hear your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes. The events took place a long time ago and it takes a little time to recall them. My question is were there any monetary incursions by Serbia in relation to the rest of Yugoslavia into the budget and was there such a danger in evidence at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are asking me to present certain assumptions, whether something could have happened in the area of financial and monetary policies. My answer may be positive or negative, but I have no grounds to claim one or the other. In answer to your previous question, after trying to recall those events, I can assure the court that the new Dinar of Bosnia-Herzegovina, though using the old bank notes, which was changed slightly with this official seal of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was in circulation quite certainly before this decree was passed in July 1992, because I was in Sarajevo at the time and I was using that currency, the so-called new Dinar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. May I draw your attention to page 53 of the same document? At the same time I should like to ask you to take a look at page 59 as well, namely if you can recall, the decision regarding establishing the criteria for defining confidential defence data on page 53 and the rules on the military ID card on page 59, in reference to these two documents, you said that they represented evidence of the functioning of a system of administration. Is that correct? Am I interpreting you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I find it difficult to quote myself and to answer with precision this question, what is probably already -- can be found in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We are not going to refer to the transcript every time, otherwise we would never get to the end. The Defence is simply asking you a question, having first said: "Am I interpreting correctly and do you agree?" If you do or you do not -- if you do agree with the interpretation that was made, then you should answer, and you can say: "I don't remember". You can say what you like, but the question is clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember what I said. I remember what my conclusion was, and I can repeat it on the basis of the documents I have before me, because my position on this has not changed, but whether the formulation of my assertion is literally word by word what I said is not important, I suppose. My assessment is that the system is functioning in practice, but the system of delegation of authority, or rather the functioning of the HVO as a government, as a cabinet with certain departments responsible for certain areas, and I established this on the basis of the fact that both of these documents you are referring to were signed now not by the President of the HVO, the President of the government, the "Prime Minister" but by the head of the appropriate department, the Defence Department in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This quantity of information or the facts that you have at your disposal surely is not sufficient for you to come to the conclusion that the system is functioning in practice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My conclusion is based on the fact that the head of the Defence Department passes or signs -- has signed two very important documents. These are not insignificant documents. They are documents on the secrecy of documents and on military ID cards. There is no need to recall here in the court how important classified information is in the armed forces, and how important a military ID card is whereby one establishes the identity of a member of the armed forces, and that is what my opinion was based on. Under other conditions, if we were talking about minor decisions, then certainly your comment would be justified.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But do not you see a difference between the definition that the system is functioning in practice and the fact that the appropriate documents have been passed? The fact that necessary documents were passed need not necessarily mean that the system is being implemented in practice. Would you agree with this way of thinking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My allegation is that the system on which the HVO is based as an organ of authority did function in practice. It delegates authority not only on the basis of Article 20 but also in the practical implementation of that authority. This system of departmental activity of the HVO is functioning in practice, otherwise these documents would still be signed by the President of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It is my submission that on the basis of the fact three, four or ten documents have been passed signed by the head of a department need not lead to the conclusion --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, defence counsel is making submissions to the court. He cannot make submissions during the cross-examination of a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, I would like to tell you for the last time, either you make rapid interpretations and ask the questions, but you cannot argue here. You are acting as if it was six months from now. At that time you can have any interpretation or opinion you want. Right now you must ask the question to the witness. He will answer. If you say: "I think this and do you agree", all right, but you cannot conduct yourself as you are. I want to tell you now for the last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am just trying to initiate a discussion and to obtain an answer. I'm not making any firm submissions, but I can put the question differently. Dr. Pajic, you are talking about a system functioning in practice. Please look to see when the key decisions were passed. On page 12 you find the decree on the armed forces. When was it passed? What date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: July 3rd, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
