utterances.text: Very good. When was the decision on the establishment of criteria for defining confidential data on page 53 through page 58 passed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 3rd July 1992. With reference -- allow me to add -- with reference to Article 10 of the previous decree on the armed forces of HZ H-B.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That is correct. When were the Rules on military ID cards on page 59 passed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also on July 3rd, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When was Bruno Stojic appointed head of the department? You have that document on page 66. The person who signed these documents, when was he appointed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May 3rd, 1992 -- sorry, sorry. 3rd July 1992. July 3rd, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Therefore, are you still claiming that the system was functioning in practice and all these documents were passed in the same day, maybe with a few minutes' difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do claim, and I repeat that a system of delegation of authority was functioning in practice within the framework of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us now go on to document 3 of Exhibit 38, page 3 of that document, document 3 of exhibit number 38. We are talking here about the District Military Prosecutors' offices. Up to then, up to the adoption of this document, the military prosecutors' offices were part of which organisation? Which organisation did the District Military Prosecutors' office belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not examine earlier documents on the basis of which I could answer this question, but I assume, considering the overall organisation of the state, that the District Military Prosecutors' offices were part either of the secretariat of the Interior, the secretariat of the Defence or the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: According to this decree, what was the nature of Military Prosecutors' Offices in terms of the time-span that they cover, and where is this indicated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the title it is stated that District Military Prosecutors' offices in times of war or the immediate threat of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who is the Military Prosecutor responsible to a military or a civilian within the HZ H-B?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to Article 4 the District Military Prosecutor is responsible for his work to the Presidency of the HZ H-B.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The civilian or military structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By definition it is the legislative body of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, but in answer to your question, the Presidency is a civilian body. However, this answer would have to be qualified by the composition of the Presidency, which included the HVO, which we have already discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please look at document 4 of Exhibit 38, page 6, the decision on border crossings. Before this decision, that is 12th November 1992, do you know who controlled the border crossings in effect, in reality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have personal knowledge, because at the time I did not use any of the listed border crossings, but being familiar with the competence of control of border crossings, those border crossings were controlled on the one side by the police of The Republic of Croatia and on the other by the police of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In 1992, after the formation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought you were asking me of the period that preceded this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Please, Mr. President, the witness must be allowed to answer the questions. Just because counsel disagrees with what he is actually saying, he can't simply keep saying. "No, no, no,".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Professor, would you please answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to, this the decision on border crossings with The Republic of Croatia Article 3, it says that: "The safety of goods and passengers at border crossings shall be ensured by the police of the Ministry of the Interior and the military police".

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am asking you before this decree was passed and after the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, who actually had control of these border crossings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only assume that they were the appropriate bodies of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know? Do you know whether the government in Sarajevo or rather the bodies of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did they control any single border crossing of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did, as far as their possibilities allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It means that there was a war and that in view of that it was difficult to maintain normal control of border crossings at all times and at all places.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am insisting. Did the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina and its government control a single border crossing of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must say again that you are asking me questions which imply that I must answer from personal knowledge. I had no personal knowledge regarding the work of the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was not a member or an employee of any state body. Therefore, I can only speak on the basis of incidental information that I heard from people who were travelling at the time, or if I personally had had occasion to see for myself what the situation was at the border crossing. On the basis of the documents that I had at my disposal for this expert opinion, I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Well, that is fine. Let me now ask you some general questions regarding these decisions that you have analysed. Correct me again if I'm wrong so we do not have to go back to the transcript again. You asserted that in certain decisions, in certain decisions, the name "Bosnia-Herzegovina" is included, namely the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is it in certain documents only or all documents, those that you analysed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When replying to this question I must make a distinction between mentioning The Republic of Herceg-Bosna in the preamble of a certain decision, which was very rare. The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in most decisions was not mentioned in the preamble. However, in most decisions the name of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina appears next to the signature of the decision in most decisions in such a way as follows. First it says The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Then in the copies I have in the Croatian language, it is underlined. The letters are highlighted "Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna" and underneath" Croatian Defence Council".

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The decisions that you studied, all of them, are they of a permanent nature or of a temporary nature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some decisions are of a temporary nature and some of a permanent nature, because by accident I have this file opened to show the document decision on border crossings with The Republic of Croatia. It does not include the provision that this is of a temporary nature, so my conclusion would be that this decision is of a permanent nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This decision, which is an exception, I draw your attention to the preamble, where one speaks of the temporary organisation of executive authority. Does that also imply temporary validity of this document, this decision, which was reached?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, I presented my analysis and expertise on this document on the basis of all the documents that were made available to me. I did not read the documents one by one and then reached a special decision on the basis of each and every document. My conclusions are based on continuity. If you look at the overall normative activity of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and later the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, you will see that there is a tendency which moves from a temporary organisation of executive authority towards permanent organisation of executive authority. Obviously there is a tendency moving from a Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna to a Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. In that way I believe that your interpretation of this preamble, that because this is the temporary organisation of executive authority that all decisions are temporary too, is too broad an interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. At this point I'm concentrating only on the decisions, and if we would move from one decision to another, what is your opinion on this basis? Are most of these decisions temporary or permanent, the decisions as enactments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By definition the decisions -- I repeat by definition the decisions that are related to the war and the immediate danger of war are of a temporary nature, because, thank God, war does not go on forever. So I do not want to confuse the two and draw a conclusion on that basis, that all decisions are of a temporary nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Also I would like to put a general question, which is not related to a specific decision, namely what was the basis for the people who founded the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna for passing this decision? We said the reasons were the war. What was the law or the right upon which they based the right to establish such a community. I do not know if I've been clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You haven't been clear enough, but in response to your question I can only quote Article 1 of the decision on the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I quote: "The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is established as the political, cultural, economic and territorial integrity".

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So the reason was to establish a separate political, cultural, economic and territorial entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That is a fundamental provision but that is not a reason. One of the reasons, if we quote this on page 2 of document 2 of Exhibit 38, we can find the unacceptability of a unitary model in multi-national communities, multi-ethnic communities, and proceeding from the constitution of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina under which Bosnia-Herzegovina was founded as a community of three constituent people: Croats, Muslims and Serbs, is that perhaps a basis on the basis of which they exercised the right to this kind of establishment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand your question, because you mentioned two contradictory quotations from the preamble. One says that The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is a unitary state. Tell me what line it is, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: 1, 2, 3, 4 ... unitary 6 model. In the first line pursuant to the constitution of The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my opinion these are two contradictory quotes from the preamble, because if Bosnia-Herzegovina was established as a community of three constituent, namely equitable peoples, Croats, Muslims and Serbs, then the other assertion is contradictory, that it was a unitary state. Then it is the question of interpretation of those who passed this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What is your opinion: the last constitution in force in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991/1992, what was the model, unitary, federal, within Bosnia-Herzegovina? ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The model of organisation of the state of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was the model of unitary organisation, but I do not give this a pejorative meaning. I wish to say that Bosnia-Herzegovina was not a decentralised state in the sense of consisting of constituent states so that it would be a federation, but I wish to remind the court of another thing, that in 1991, after the elections in November 1990, Bosnia-Herzegovina was given full legitimacy as the state of three constituent peoples, whose national political parties won a majority in the elections, specifically the Croatian Democratic Union, the political party of the Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina; the Party of Democratic Action, the party of the Muslim people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the Serbian Democratic Party, the party of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and on the basis of these elections at the end of 1990 a Coalition Government of these three partners who won majority in Parliament was established, that is to say that from the point of view of internal law and constitutional law the equal rights of the constituent peoples Bosnia-Herzegovina was reiterated, and I wish to remind you of an amendment from 1991. In the Parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina a special mechanism was set up for bringing into question all those laws for which any ethnic group presented in Parliament would claim that it jeopardises their national interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: According to the Dayton constitution -- I imagine that, of course, due to the nature of your work, you are familiar with it -- is The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina a unitary or federal state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not want to initiate an academic debate on that here, but according to the Dayton accords Bosnia and Herzegovina denies definition, because it is a state consisting of two entities. Bosnia and Herzegovina itself is not called a republic any longer, because in Article 1 of the Dayton agreement or the Dayton constitution it is said that The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina will continue its legal existence as Bosnia-Herzegovina and that it shall consist of two entries, out of which one is called Republika Srpska and the other is called the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, you have a very strange legal situation whereby there is a state which consists of one republic and of one federation. Again, I'm sorry. I do not want to go into an academic debate now, but I just want to show the extent to which this notion has not been defined.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: At any rate it's not unitary. I wish to draw your attention to document 7, page 7, too. So document 7, page 7 speaks of the flag and the coat of arms. The coat of arms and the flag. Let us define it immediately. Is it a permanent or a temporary document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The decree is valid in times of war or immediate threat of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You highlighted this example as an example of elements of statehood, and I ask you at that time whether Bosnia and Herzegovina had a flag of its own, and does it have a flag today, a federal flag?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In November 1992 -- accidentally this happens to be the month when this decree was passed -- in November 1992 I attended a conference in New York and in front of the UN building I saw the flag of Bosnia-Herzegovina flying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I'm asking you as a Professor of law whether the constitution and law establish what the flag of Bosnia-Herzegovina is then in 1992 or today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the definite text from 1993, stipulates the flag of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This flag was decided upon previously by the amendments to that constitution, but I cannot tell you exactly when that was, but I emphasise once again, because you are asking me, from the point of view of international law, the flag of a state is that state which is internationally recognised, and not to go now into any kind of subjective discussion, that is the flag that I found in front of the United Nations building in New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is that flag accepted today, recognised today in a legal and formal sense?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is well-known that the Dayton agreement did not decide on that, and negotiations are still being held between the two entities or three peoples Bosnia-Herzegovina on establishing a common flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The flag and coat of arms is what you highlighted as a characteristic of statehood. Do you think that this right to a coat of arms and flag exclusively belongs to a state, or can other organisations also have a coat of arms and a flag?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course non-state entities can also have a flag, but, as I explained yesterday or the day before yesterday in one of the answers put to me by one of the honourable judges, it is customary, and I believe in certain states it is regulated by law, too, if a regional flag is flown or a city flag or a provincial flag on official occasions the State flag is always flown in addition to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there such a law in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina never recognised the flag of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I recall the decision of the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1992, when all of these regulations were declared anti-constitutional. So Bosnia-Herzegovina never expressed its views on the flag of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please move on to Document 8 of 38, pages 1 and 2, where reference is made to military --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The page, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The first page and the second page. That is already Official Gazette number 2. Military industry is referred to here, industry for special purposes, as you mentioned before. Before this decree was passed, from a formal, legal point of view, who was the owner of the military industry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The problem of ownership in the former Yugoslavia from the point of view of modern legal terminology well-known throughout the world is rather difficult to define. You know that there was always this contradiction between social ownership, private ownership. Social ownership from a legal point of view was very difficult to compare to any category of ownership and property existing in a democratic system. Therefore, it is hard for me to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I shall re-word it, re-phrase it. Who managed the military industry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The military industry was managed by the administrative organs in charge of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Of the republic or the federation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is not a subject matter in which I'm an expert, so I do not want to go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please let us move on to document 9 of Exhibit 38, and I wish to draw your attention to page 2, the decree on the application of the law and regular courts. So page 2, document 9. As usual, I ask the question: is this a temporary or permanent decree -- sorry. I'm hurrying again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The decree was passed to be valid in times of immediate threat of war or in wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The next question. If you are aware of this, in 1992, 1993 and 1994 how were judges elected in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, if you are familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This decree, does it basically speak of anything else except the appointment of judges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This decree is characteristic for me, because it speaks of the right of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna to establish and abolish courts; also that the Croatian Defence Council decides on the number of judges and lay judges, and finally, that the Presidency of the HZ H-B elects and recalls judges and lay judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please let us move on to document 10 of Exhibit 38, page 6. That is the decree on border crossing. If you allow me --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: May we have a moment, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We have a translation problem with respect to the pagination, and I would like to make Mr. Nobilo aware of it so perhaps the English translation is consistent with the pagination of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Registrar, I was on 10, the decree of 26th February 1993, having to do with border crossing. Is that what you are talking about, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes. It is just that the English translation is resulting on pages that are beyond the length of the document. So there's some misunderstanding or miscommunication between Mr. Nobilo and the translator, and I would like to alert him to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reason for the confusion is actually because Mr. Nobilo is actually referring to the volume number rather than the page number, but frankly it doesn't really make any difference because he is also referring to the number of the document, which is quite clear. For example, on this document, he refers to page 6. It is, in fact, page 122, but it really makes no difference, apart from the clarity, which I perfectly accept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Yes, I agree with the Prosecutor. I have been getting along this way for quite a while now, because I think there is a certain degree of ambiguity, but I'm getting along even that much better because it is a decree that wasn't even translated into French. So ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I do not have that number of pages. I have the original page, so I'm trying to identify the page concerned in each exhibit. So now we are on document 10, original page 6, the decree on border crossing. In this context I would like to read Article 2 and would you kindly comment on that? I do not think you commented on that and I think it is important. So Article 2: "The border area shall consist of a part of the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina hereinafter referred to as "HB H" within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, hereinafter referred to as HZ H-B, including the mainland, river, lakes and seas along the borderline, that is a 100 metre wide belt". Can you put that in the context of your comment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My comment was that this decree actually referring to the border between The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- the border between The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and The Republic of Croatia is the area that is actually being referred to here -- is taken over by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, because Article 7 says clearly: "The HVO HZ H-B shall designate the international border crossings and the local border crossings". So in that context it seemed to me that this Article, too, was there actually pro forma in this decree, and that effectively in terms of establishing the true border crossing regime, all the competence falls within the jurisdiction of the HVO of the HZ H-B.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I agree as far as jurisdiction is concerned, but why don't you interpret it bona fide? The border of the HZ H-B towards Croatia, isn't that at the same time the border towards The Republic of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Article 12 was also extensively discussed on the next page. I would like to read it out: "A citizen in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina carrying weapons and ammunition into or out of the HZ H-B shall report the weapons and ammunition to the border police or the military police at the state border". I will immediately read Article 13, too, where it says: "Foreign citizens shall report the weapons and ammunition they carry with them to the border police or military police upon crossing of the border. Foreign citizens may bring into the HZ H-B side weapons and ammunition for these weapons provided they have an authorisation for them from the relevant organs of the state whose citizens they are". Kindly interpret these two articles. Who is a foreigner and who is a citizen of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the HZ H-B?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No. I mean who is a foreigner when crossing a border? For example, in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, who is treated as a foreigner and who is treated as a citizen of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because we only have two categories. We don't have any citizens of HZ H-B. So how do you interpret Articles 12 and 13 in relation to the existence of a citizen of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the category of foreigner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I explained yesterday that this provision implicitly -- I repeat this provision implicitly says that a citizen of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is treated as a foreigner. Although this is not explicitly said, this is implicitly said. Why? Because paragraph 2 of Article 12 requires for persons from paragraph 1 too, that is a citizen of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, approval of the competent body of HVO HZ H-B. So from the point of view of authorisation, a foreigner and a citizen of The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina have to have authorisation for carrying such a weapon across the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Isn't that only natural, because we are talking about weapons, not a normal border crossing? That is one question. The second question is: do you not notice that there is not a third category, for example citizens of the HZ H-B; only two categories, the citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina and a foreigner. One excludes the other. How can you say --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry to intervene again, but learned counsel is asking one question after another. The witness is not allowed to answer. He may wish to establish a point. He may be hearing answers he doesn't like, but he must allow the witness to actually answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You must be concerned by the fact that time is moving along quickly. First, ask the first question. Sometimes you even answer instead of the witness, which is, of course, your right, but do allow him to answer as well. This gives me the opportunity to set the schedule for the rest of the cross-examination. Ask your first question first and then your second.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I try to move as fast as possible and to put together two interrelated questions, but we can proceed in that way, too, although we'll require a lot more time that way. Well, how do you interpret the fact that there are only two categories of citizens, foreigners and citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Professor, answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this point in time it is clear that here, and I didn't even imply that -- one cannot speak of citizenship of the HZ HB. It is true that this provision speaks of citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but I emphasise that this wording implicitly says that a citizen of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina has a somewhat different status when crossing the border or when on the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. That was my point. With your permission, I would like to link this to Article 18 of the same decree, where it says: "Citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina may move and sojourn in the border area only if they have an appropriate permit". Why do citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina have to have a permit in order to move in the border area on the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Wasn't there the same kind of regulation in Yugoslavia on the special status of the border area where those who do not live in the border area could not move quite freely? Are you familiar with these regulations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with these regulations. I have often travelled throughout Yugoslavia and I did not encounter such status.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: One thing is a border crossing. Another thing is a border area near the border but without a border crossing. It has a special status. Do you remember these regulations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember these regulations, but I find your terminology clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you accept what I said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That there can be a difference? I cannot refer to a concrete regulation or rule in this sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayman? The time has come to adjourn our hearing. We will resume tomorrow morning. I suppose that causes some problems for Professor Pajic, as you said, but unfortunately I'm not quite sure what we can do to change it. First, turning to the Defence, next morning, which is the last of the week, do you think that you will be able to complete your questions tomorrow? I know that you ask several at the same time in order to speed things up, but for the Presiding Judge you have to try to summarise things somewhat. Do you think that tomorrow morning would be enough for you, Mr. Nobilo, and Mr. Hayman, to complete your cross-examination? Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We will certainly finish tomorrow, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I am turning to the Prosecutor before speaking to the witness. Mr. Cayley, what do you suggest to us, in agreement with the witness, who may have to remain.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The witness will remain tomorrow, Mr. President. As you are aware, the rules of procedure allow for a re-examination by the Prosecutor after cross-examination by the Defence. I believe that will be a short and concise process, but I would imagine if the Defence finish within two hours tomorrow, one and a half hours, we would be able to finish with Dr. Pajic tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What I first would like to suggest -- let me thank Professor Pajic. We know that you have commitments and you have accepted -- you have agreed to stay, as I asked you and my colleagues asked you. We thank for that. Tomorrow morning, therefore. So we will complete this tomorrow morning. If you agree, I would like to apologise with the interpreters, we could start at 9.30 tomorrow, so we would have some margin knowing we might be over at 1 o'clock. I am asking the Defence and the Prosecutor to complete tomorrow -- what you have to do tomorrow morning. This is a friendly but firm request. If you can't, you can't, but I really do ask you for the conduct of the proceedings to do your best. We will start tomorrow at 9.30. Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: --ooOoo--
